title: Pawn races
summary: Count the tempi, queen with check, put the new queen to work and know when not to race.
part.count.title: Counting the tempi
part.count.summary: Who queens first, and why that only wins when the new queen watches the other queening square.
step.t_race: Both pawns are passed, and neither king can stop the other pawn in time: the black king is far from the h-pawn, and the white king would have to get past the black king to reach the a-pawn. It is a real race. White to move. Count each side's moves to promotion. Who queens first, and is that enough?
step.t_race.hint1: The h2 pawn may advance two squares on its first move. Count how many moves it needs to reach h8, and how many the a7 pawn needs to reach a1.
step.t_race.hint2: Both of them queen. Look at the diagonal that starts on h8 and see where it ends.
step.tempo: Now count. With 1.h4, my pawn needs five moves to reach h8. The black pawn also needs five to reach a1. I move first, so I queen first. That alone does not win: queen against queen is usually a draw. What wins is that my queen on h8 watches a1 along the diagonal: the black queen is born and captured. With 1.h3? I would lose a tempo and it would be a draw. And it has to be a queen: a bishop on h8 would also capture on a1, but king and bishop cannot mate.
step.d_race: Both pawns have already moved two squares each, and I am still one tempo ahead. Count with me, move by move.
step.d_race.m1: 1.h6: two moves to queen. The black king can neither reach my pawn nor help its own.
step.d_race.m2: 1...a3: the black pawn reaches the third rank. Two to go for it as well, but the next move is mine.
step.d_race.m3: 2.h7: I queen next move. Notice that h8 and a1 lie on the same diagonal.
step.d_race.m4: 2...a2: the black pawn will queen too, and it is born precisely on a1.
step.d_race.m5: 3.h8=Q: the queen is born eyeing a1. The square where the black queen will be born is already covered.
step.d_race.m6: 3...a1=Q: the black queen is born on a square I control. It will live for one move only.
step.d_race.m7: 4.Qxa1: captured on the very next move. Queen against king: the rest is technique.
step.raceMove: Your turn. White to move and win. Do the count and race with the right pawn in the right way.
step.raceMove.hint: Do not waste time: the h2 pawn can move two squares. And no king move helps here.
step.raceMove.done: That's it. You stay a tempo ahead, and the queen will be born on h8, eyeing a1.
part.check.title: Queening with check
part.check.summary: A queen born with check wins the missing tempo; sometimes it is even worth giving up one queen so that the other is born with check.
step.t_check: Both pawns run, and neither king can reach the other pawn. Count, then look at where the black king stands. What can the white queen do the moment it is born?
step.t_check.hint1: The a4 pawn queens on a8. Trace the diagonal from a8 to h1 and see who is on it.
step.t_check.hint2: Queening with check gains a move. With that move, the queen reaches the square where the black pawn wants to queen.
step.checkWhy: The black king is on f3, on the long diagonal. When my pawn queens on a8, the queen arrives with check. Black spends the move on the king, and I use mine to put the queen on h1, in front of the black pawn. Queening with check is worth a tempo. Only 1.a5 wins: any king move lets Black run first.
step.d_check: The pawns have already run: mine is on a6, the black one on h3, and the count is level, each two moves from queening. See how the check decides.
step.d_check.m1: 1.a7: one move to go. If I were to queen without check, Black would queen as well.
step.d_check.m2: 1...h2: one move to h1. Now count whose turn it is.
step.d_check.m3: 2.a8=Q+: queen with check along the a8–h1 diagonal, because the king on f3 stands on it. Black's move will be a king move, not a pawn move.
step.d_check.m4: 2...Kg3: the king steps out of check and protects the pawn.
step.d_check.m5: 3.Qh1: the queen sits on the queening square. The pawn will never move again, and my king comes to capture it.
step.d_sac: One step further. Here, if I queen on h8 at once, 1.h8=Q? d1=Q+ and it is a draw. But I have two promotions, and one of them can serve just to give the check.
step.d_sac.m1: 1.f8=Q+: I give up the queen with check. The king has to capture it and lands on f8, on the rank where my other pawn queens.
step.d_sac.m2: 1...Kxf8, forced. The black king now stands on the eighth rank.
step.d_sac.m3: 2.h8=Q+: the second queen is born with check. That is the tempo the first one bought.
step.d_sac.m4: 2...Ke7: the king steps away, and the d-pawn is still on d2.
step.d_sac.m5: 3.Qd4: the queen reaches the d-file before the pawn queens. If it steps to d1, I capture it. A won ending.
step.checkMove: White to move and win. The black pawn is one step from queening. Use the check.
step.checkMove.hint: Queen on the square where the new queen gives check at once. Then stop the black pawn on its queening square.
step.checkMove.done: Perfect. The queen was born with check and went to h1. Now the white king walks over and the pawn falls.
part.skewer.title: Two queens on the board
part.skewer.summary: When both sides queen, the skewering check wins the other queen; if the king is not on the line, the first check drives it there.
step.t_skewer: Both pawns queen, one after the other, and neither queen will watch the other's square. What happens the moment both queens are on the board?
step.t_skewer.hint1: Look at the b-file: who will be standing on it after both promotions?
step.t_skewer.hint2: A check that goes straight through the king and reaches the piece behind it.
step.skewerWhy: After 1.f7 b2 2.f8=Q b1=Q, neither queen watches the other's square: from f8 you cannot see b1. But the black king stands on b5 and its queen was born on b1, on the same file. 3.Qb8+ checks through the king: it has to step aside, and the queen on b1 is captured. That is the skewer, the most common weapon when both sides queen. And only 1.f7 wins: a king move now would let Black queen first.
step.d_skewer: The white pawn is already on f7 and the black one on b2. Watch the skewer.
step.d_skewer.m1: 1.f8=Q: I queen first, without check and without watching b1. It looks like little.
step.d_skewer.m2: 1...b1=Q: two queens, it looks drawn. Look at the b-file.
step.d_skewer.m3: 2.Qb8+: check on the file. Behind the king, on the same file, stands the queen on b1.
step.d_skewer.m4: 2...Kc4: the king has to leave the file; any square comes to the same.
step.d_skewer.m5: 3.Qxb1: the queen is captured. The check went through the king: a skewer.
step.d_drive: And when the king is not on its queen's line? Here the black king is on e1 and the queen on a2: no immediate skewer. Look for the check that forces the king onto its queen's rank.
step.d_drive.m1: 1.Qh1+: check on the first rank. The king only has squares on the second rank, its own queen's rank.
step.d_drive.m2: 1...Kd2: the king steps onto its queen's rank. 1...Ke2 would come to the same.
step.d_drive.m3: 2.Qh2+: check on the second rank, with the queen on a2 behind the king.
step.d_drive.m4: 2...Kc3: the king leaves the rank and leaves the queen on a2 undefended.
step.d_drive.m5: 3.Qxa2: the queen is captured. The first check drives, the second one skewers.
step.skewerMove: Now you, in the same position. White to move and win: drive the king onto its queen's line and skewer.
step.skewerMove.hint: The king on the edge only has squares on the second rank. Where is its queen?
step.skewerMove.done: That's it. The first check drove, the second one skewered: the black queen is gone.
part.trade.title: Trading the queens
part.trade.summary: With an extra pawn, queen first and force the queen trade with checks: the pawn ending is won. Nesterov–Zolnierowicz, 1993.
step.tradeWhy: This is Nesterov against Zolnierowicz, Katowice, 1993. Both kings stood in front of their pawns; Nesterov ran the f-pawn and both sides queened: 51.f8=Q b1=Q. Without queens the ending is his: the white king stands next to the h6 pawn and the black king is far away. So he does not try to win the queen, and 52.Qxh6? would only draw: he gives checks that drive the black king next to the queen on b1 and trades with 56.Qxb1+. In the game, after 52.Qc5+ Kd2 53.Qf2+, Zolnierowicz resigned. Watch the whole ladder.
step.d_trade: The ladder of checks, move by move. Only 52.Qc5+ wins; the other moves draw, and some even lose.
step.d_trade.m1: 52.Qc5+: check along the diagonal. 52.Qxh6? would only draw: what I want is the black king next to its queen.
step.d_trade.m2: 52...Kd2: the king drops to the second rank, as Zolnierowicz played.
step.d_trade.m3: 53.Qf2+: check on the second rank. The king has to go back to the third rank or down to the first.
step.d_trade.m4: 53...Kc3: Zolnierowicz had already resigned, right after 53.Qf2+. See what was coming.
step.d_trade.m5: 54.Qd4+: check again. The king only has b3 and c2, ever closer to b1.
step.d_trade.m6: 54...Kb3: the king goes to b3, still trying to stay away from its queen.
step.d_trade.m7: 55.Qb6+: check on the b-file. The black king must stay next to b1, on a2 or c2; if it goes far away, its queen is captured for nothing.
step.d_trade.m8: 55...Kc2: the king guards the queen. There is no other defence.
step.d_trade.m9: 56.Qxb1+: a trade with check. The king has to recapture, leaving a pawn ending in which my king goes to f5, g6 and captures h6. The h-pawn queens on its own.
step.d_tradePawns: After 56...Kxb1 the pawn ending remains. See why it is won: my king reaches the h6 pawn and the black king gets nowhere.
step.d_tradePawns.m1: 57.Kf5: on the way to g6, from where I attack h6. A king going to the d-file would only draw.
step.d_tradePawns.m2: 57...Kc2: the black king runs, but it is many squares away from my pawn.
step.d_tradePawns.m3: 58.Kg6: I attack the h6 pawn, which has no one to defend it.
step.d_tradePawns.m4: 58...Kd3: the black king keeps coming, far too late.
step.d_tradePawns.m5: 59.Kxh6: I capture the pawn. Now it is king and pawn against king, with my king in front of the pawn.
step.d_tradePawns.m6: 59...Ke4: the black king comes, but my king steps out of the pawn's way and escorts it to h8.
step.d_tradePawns.m7: 60.Kg7: I clear the way. The h-pawn walks to h8 with no one to stop it.
step.tradeMove: Play like Nesterov, from 51...b1=Q. White to move and win: the ladder of checks up to the trade.
step.tradeMove.hint: Check after check, always pushing the black king towards its own queen; at the end, capture on b1 with check.
step.tradeMove.done: That's it. The queens are gone and the white king goes for the h6 pawn: a won ending.
part.catch.title: Hunt instead of racing
part.catch.summary: So far the race has happened. Before racing, see whether your king captures the other pawn; against two pawns, first keep them together.
step.catchWhy: So far the race has always happened. Now, before racing, ask: do I really have to? Racing with 1.a5? draws: both sides queen and it is queen against queen. But look at the distances: my king reaches e2 in three moves, the f-pawn needs three to queen, and it is my move. The black king on h7 cannot reach my a-pawn. So I hunt first, and the a-pawn walks in by itself afterwards.
step.d_catch: Watch the hunt. The king reaches e2 in three moves; 1.a5? would only draw.
step.d_catch.m1: 1.Kc3: one step towards e2, along the lower ranks. 1.Kc2 and 1.Kc4 work as well.
step.d_catch.m2: 1...f3: the pawn runs. Two more moves to f1.
step.d_catch.m3: 2.Kd2: two moves from f1, with Black to move.
step.d_catch.m4: 2...f2: one move to queen. But my king already reaches f1.
step.d_catch.m5: 3.Ke2: I watch f1. The pawn can only queen to be captured.
step.d_catch.m6: 3...f1=Q+: the queen is born with check, but on a square I control.
step.d_catch.m7: 4.Kxf1: I capture the queen. The black king will never reach my a-pawn: hunting beat racing.
step.d_restrain: Now the other side has two pawns, and mine is on h3. Any king move that does not attack g7 lets the black pawns advance to h5 and g5 and break free: a draw. The idea, which Grigoriev used in a 1931 study: first keep the pawns together, within the king's reach; only then think about racing.
step.d_restrain.m1: 1.h4: pins both pawns down. 1...g5 would now be met by 2.hxg5, and 1...h5 leaves the g7 pawn behind. 1.Kf7, attacking g7 at once, would win as well.
step.d_restrain.m2: 1...h5: Black splits the pawns. The g-pawn is left alone and behind.
step.d_restrain.m3: 2.Kf5: the king heads for g5, from where it attacks h5 and watches g6, the square the g7 pawn would have to cross.
step.d_restrain.m4: 2...Kb3: the black king runs towards my pawn, but it is much too far.
step.d_restrain.m5: 3.Kg5: I attack the h5 pawn, which no one defends.
step.d_restrain.m7: 4.Kxh5: one pawn captured. The other, on g7, is within my king's reach.
step.d_restrain.m8: 4...Kd5: the black king is still four moves from h4.
step.d_restrain.m9: 5.Kg6: I attack g7. It falls next move, and my h-pawn queens by itself.
step.catchMove: Now you, in the same position as the hunt. White to move and win: take the king to the f-pawn, and don't hurry with the a-pawn.
step.catchMove.hint: The f4 pawn will queen on f1. Head for e2 or f1 with the king, along the lower ranks.
step.catchMove.done: Exactly. The king gets there in time to capture the f-pawn, and the black king will never reach your a-pawn. Hunting beat racing.
part.line.title: The line of the check
part.line.summary: Whoever stays on the line of the queen about to be born gets checked and loses his own queen. The king steps off it; on the other side, the piece standing on the line blocks the check.
step.t_line: Now you are Black. The count is yours: your h-pawn gets there first. And yet running all the way loses. Why, and what should you do?
step.t_line.hint1: Trace the diagonal from a8 to h1 and see who is on it.
step.t_line.hint2: The king can do two useful things at once: leave a line and get closer to something.
step.diagonal: Your king stands on d5, on the a8–h1 diagonal. If you run all the way, 1...h3 2.a6 h2? 3.a7 h1=Q 4.a8=Q+, and the queen on h1 is captured along the same diagonal. The way out is to step off the diagonal with the king and, while you are at it, go after the a-pawn: 1...h3 and, after 2.a6, 2...Kc6.
step.d_lineErr: Switch sides for a moment. Black has gone wrong: with my pawn already on a6, they pushed their pawn to h2 instead of taking the king off the diagonal. Watch the punishment.
step.d_lineErr.m1: 1.a7: the white pawn does not stop. Black queens first, but that no longer matters.
step.d_lineErr.m2: 1...h1=Q: Black queens, and the new queen sits on h1, at the end of the diagonal.
step.d_lineErr.m3: 2.a8=Q+: the white queen is born with check along the diagonal where the black king stayed.
step.d_lineErr.m4: 2...Kd4: the king has to step aside; any square comes to the same.
step.d_lineErr.m5: 3.Qxh1: the queen on h1 is captured along the same diagonal. One king move at the right time would have avoided it all.
step.blocked: On the other side, the same line can save you. This is the end of a study by Moravec, 1950: Black has queened, the white king has fled to c8 and the c6 pawn holds the draw. The black queen wants 1...Qg4+, which would win that pawn. But the black king stands on f3, on the d1–g4 diagonal, and blocks its own check. With the king on f2, 1...Qg4+ would win. The defender, then, tries to put the enemy king on that square: that is for the test.
step.diagonalMove: Black again: play and win. The first move may be the pawn's; after that, mind the diagonal.
step.diagonalMove.hint: After 1...h3 2.a6, do not carry on with 2...h2. The black king leaves the diagonal and heads for the a-pawn.
step.diagonalMove.done: Well done. The king left the diagonal and will capture the pawn. Racing on with 2...h2 would have lost to 3.a7 h1=Q 4.a8=Q+.
part.block.title: The king that bars the way
part.block.summary: The king stepped off the line; now it stands in the other king's way: before racing, it closes his way back to your pawn.
step.blockWhy: The f-pawn runs and the a-pawn is slow: it looks like an easy race. But 1.f4? lets the black king come back: 1...Kb5, then 2.f5 Kc5 3.f6 Kd6, and it enters the square of the f-pawn. My pawn needs four moves, and he gets there. 1.Kc4 takes b5, b4 and b3 away from the black king: it only has a3 and a5, far from the path, and the a6 pawn is far too slow to worry me. First the king bars; then the pawn runs.
step.d_blockErr: First the mistake. White raced with 1.f4, and the black king comes back. Watch which way.
step.d_blockErr.m1: 1...Kb5: the king walks through the door that was left open.
step.d_blockErr.m2: 2.f5: the pawn carries on; it is too late to bar the way.
step.d_blockErr.m3: 2...Kc5: one more square towards the pawn's square.
step.d_blockErr.m4: 3.f6: two moves to queen, and the black king almost there.
step.d_blockErr.m5: 3...Kd6: the king enters the square of the f6 pawn. Now it reaches f8.
step.d_blockErr.m6: 4.f7: one move to queen, but it is Black's turn.
step.d_blockErr.m7: 4...Ke7: the pawn is stopped for good. A draw, and the a6 pawn did not even need to move.
step.d_block: Now the right way: the king shuts the door and only then the pawn runs.
step.d_block.m1: 1.Kc4: I close b3, b4 and b5. The black king can only move along the a-file.
step.d_block.m2: 1...Ka5: the king tries to come round the top, via a5 and b6.
step.d_block.m3: 2.Kc5: I close b6 and b5 as well. It stays stuck on the a-file.
step.d_block.m4: 2...Ka4: back it goes. It is the only square left.
step.d_block.m5: 3.f4: now the pawn runs, and the black king has no way back.
step.d_block.m6: 3...Kb3: the king tries underneath, too late.
step.d_block.m7: 4.f5: three moves to queen, and the black king still on b3.
step.d_block.m8: 4...Kc2: the black king can reach neither my pawn nor its square.
step.d_block.m9: 5.f6: two moves, with the black king outside the square. The pawn queens, and the a6 pawn has not even moved.
step.blockMove: White to move and win. Bar first, race second.
step.blockMove.hint: The black king wants to come back via b5. Which square for your king takes b3, b4 and b5 away from it at once?
step.blockMove.done: That's it. The black king is stuck on the a-file, and now the pawn runs with no worry. In the test you will do the same as Black.
part.zigzag.title: The zigzag king
part.zigzag.summary: The escorting king never steps on the square where the other pawn checks with tempo; at the end, it forces his king onto the queening diagonal.
step.zigzagWhy: Check. The position comes from an exercise in the study the test uses: the white king has already driven the black king away, and the h-pawn is about to run. 1.Kd3? looks natural, but after 1...Kb3 2.h5 comes 2...c4+ right when it hurts: 3.Kd2 Kb2 4.h6 c3+, the pawn advances twice with check, and Black gains the tempi it needed to draw. 1.Ke3 heads for the same d2, but outside the squares where the pawn gives check: that is the zigzag, and those squares are the mined squares of the books.
step.d_zigzagErr: First the mistake: White stepped out of check with 1.Kd3, the square where the c-pawn will give check. Watch the punishment.
step.d_zigzagErr.m1: 1...Kb3: the black king escorts its pawn and waits for the check.
step.d_zigzagErr.m2: 2.h5: the pawn runs, but Black's move comes with check.
step.d_zigzagErr.m3: 2...c4+: check. The king has to spend a move, and that move belonged to the h-pawn.
step.d_zigzagErr.m4: 3.Kd2: to guard c1. But the black king gets there first.
step.d_zigzagErr.m5: 3...Kb2: now 4.h6 c3+ comes with check again, and Black queens in time. A draw.
step.d_zigzag: Now the right path: the king zigzags and, at the end, the move that decides.
step.d_zigzag.m1: 1.Ke3: out of range of a pawn check on c4. The pawn may advance, but without check.
step.d_zigzag.m2: 1...Kb3: the black king escorts its pawn, waiting for a check.
step.d_zigzag.m3: 2.h5: every move of his king is a pawn move for me.
step.d_zigzag.m4: 2...c4: the pawn advances, but without check. My king is not on d3.
step.d_zigzag.m5: 3.h6: one more pawn move. Two to go to h8.
step.d_zigzag.m6: 3...c3: no check again. My king is on e3.
step.d_zigzag.m7: 4.h7: one move to queen, and it is Black's turn.
step.d_zigzag.m8: 4...c2: one move to queen as well. But if I queen now, 5.h8=Q? c1=Q and it is a draw.
step.d_zigzag.m9: 5.Kd2: I attack the c2 pawn. The black king has to guard c1, and to do so it steps to b2, onto the h8 diagonal.
step.d_zigzag.m10: 5...Kb2: the only move. Otherwise the c2 pawn is captured.
step.d_zigzag.m11: 6.h8=Q+: the queen is born with check, and c1 will never happen.
step.zigzagMove: Now you, from the check. White to move and win: step out of check the right way and run.
step.zigzagMove.hint: Do not step on the square where the c-pawn would give check next move.
step.zigzagMove.done: That's it. The c-pawn advances without check, and your h-pawn gets there first. In the test, Grigoriev asks for the same zigzag with the white king.
part.behind.title: When the pawn reaches the seventh
part.behind.summary: And when the count does not add up? A bishop's pawn on the seventh still saves the game, as Fischer showed. Then the rules and the practical challenge.
step.fischer: Now you are the one arriving late. This is Petrosian against Fischer, Portorož Interzonal, 1958, round 13, with Black to move. The white pawn threatens to queen next move. The game stopped here, after 67.f7, and the two agreed a draw. Fischer's analysis shows why: 67...Rxg6+ 68.Kxg6 Kb1 69.f8=Q c2. White queens first, but the bishop's pawn reaches the seventh with its king alongside, and the white king is too far away: when the queen captures the pawn, the black king will be stalemated in the corner. Whoever loses the race still runs, with the right pawn.
step.d_fischerGame: Fischer's analysis, from the final position of the game. You play Black.
step.d_fischerGame.m1: 67...Rxg6+: the rook gives itself up for the g6 pawn, so that only the f-pawn remains against my c-pawn.
step.d_fischerGame.m2: 68.Kxg6: the white king captures, and stays far from the a1 corner.
step.d_fischerGame.m3: 68...Kb1: the king goes next to the pawn, without blocking the c2 square.
step.d_fischerGame.m4: 69.f8=Q: White queens first. Now it is queen against pawn.
step.d_fischerGame.m5: 69...c2: the bishop's pawn reaches the seventh, guarded by the king. This is the position that saves the game.
step.d_fischer: After 69...c2, White tries everything. Carry on as Black and notice where the king stays.
step.d_fischer.m1: 70.Qb4+: the queen wants to drive the king to c1, in front of the pawn.
step.d_fischer.m2: 70...Ka2: the king stays beside the pawn, never in front.
step.d_fischer.m3: 71.Qc3: the queen attacks the pawn. Left undefended, it is captured.
step.d_fischer.m4: 71...Kb1: defends, and the king is still beside it.
step.d_fischer.m5: 72.Qb3+: another check, to drive the king off b1 and force it to c1.
step.d_fischer.m6: 72...Ka1: the corner! If the queen captures the pawn, there is no move left at all.
step.d_fischer.m7: 73.Qxc2: stalemate. The white king was too far away to help; with it close by, the queen would win.
step.recap: Three rules to take into the practical challenge. First: count each pawn's moves, with the double step and the turn; and before racing, see whether your king can capture the other pawn or bar his king's way back. Second: queening first only wins if the new queen does something on the very next move: check, watch the other queening square, skewer or trade the other queen. Third: the king never stays on the line of the queen about to be born, and never steps on the square where the other pawn checks with tempo.
step.finish: Now play it to the end. Count, queen first and put the queen to work.
ex.e11: The race is over: both queens are on the board, and it is White to move. Find the winning move.
ex.e11.hint: The black king is on the a-file and its queen is on b1. Which file can a check force the king onto?
ex.e11.solution: 1.Qa8+! The king only has squares on the b-file (1...Kb4, 1...Kb5 or 1...Kb6), and then 2.Qb8+ (2.Qb7+ works too) is a skewer: the king leaves the file and 3.Qxb1. Had Black been to move, Black would have traded the queens. Position from the study "Pawn Races" by njswift.
ex.e12: Najdorf–Vinueza, 1941. White threatens 69.Ke2 to stop your pawn. Where does your king go? Find the draw.
ex.e12.hint: The white pawn will queen on b8. Which diagonal leaves b8? Then think about what saves a bishop pawn when the queen is born first.
ex.e12.solution: 68...Kh3! On g3 the king would stand on the b8–h2 diagonal, and the new queen would arrive with check; 68...f4 also loses. After 69.b5 f4, and when the white king comes with 70.Ke4, 70...Kg3! The bishop pawn reaches the second rank with its king beside it, and with the white king far away the queen cannot win (the bishop-pawn stalemate, as in Petrosian–Fischer).
ex.e13: Running with the pawn right away looks natural. What does the white king want to do? Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: The white king wants to come back along the long diagonal to catch the f-pawn. Who closes its path?
ex.e13.solution: 1...Kd5! After 1...f5? the white king comes back with 2.Kb4 and 3.Kc3 and arrives in time. After 2.Kb4, 2...Kd4! The white king stands in front of its own pawn and has no way back; then 3...f5 (or 3...Kd5) and the race belongs to Black. At the end the white king lands on f1's diagonal, and the promotion on f1 arrives with check and wins the other queen. Position from the study "Pawn Races" by njswift.
ex.e14: Nesterov–Zolnierowicz, 1993. Both kings stand in front of their pawns. Which king move? Find the winning move.
ex.e14.hint: Both sides will queen. Think about what the white queen does right after the black one appears on b1, and about the h-pawn that remains.
ex.e14.solution: 46.Ke5! (46.Ke4 and 46.Kf5 draw.) The pawn runs and queens first: 47.f4, 48.f5, 49.f6, 50.f7, 51.f8=Q, and after 51...b1=Q the checks 52.Qc5+, 53.Qf2+, 54.Qd4+ and 55.Qb6+ drive the black king until the queen on b1 falls or is traded (56.Qxb1+). What is left is a pawn ending in which the white king, close to the h-pawn, wins.
ex.e15: Study by Grigoriev, 1931. Black has an extra pawn. Only one move wins, and then two more. Find the winning move.
ex.e15.hint: The black pawns can move two squares. And when the white pawn queens on g8, which diagonal is the black king on a2 sitting on?
ex.e15.solution: 1.h4! keeps the black pawns together, within reach of the king (1.h3 draws). After 1...h5, 2.Kf8! and not 2.Kf7: the king must stay off the a2–g8 diagonal and off the g-file. After 2...g6, 3.Ke7! (3.Kf7, 3.Kg7, 3.Ke8 and 3.Kg8 draw). Then 3...g5 4.hxg5 h4 5.g6 h3 6.g7 h2 and 7.g8=Q+: the queen is born checking the king on a2 and gets there before the h-pawn.
ex.e16: Study by Grigoriev, 1931. White is ahead, but every move has to be exact. Find the winning move.
ex.e16.hint: The a-pawn can move two squares, sometimes with check. Which squares should the white king avoid, and along which path does it reach b7?
ex.e16.solution: 1.c4! and 2.c5! The pawn moves before the black king arrives (1.Kc5? blocks its own pawn). Then the king zigzags: 3.Ka5!, 4.Ka6! and only then 5.Kb5!, when the black king can no longer go to d5. On b5 too early comes 3...a6+ or 3...Kd5. After 6.Kc6 and 7.Kb7 both sides queen, but 10.c8=Q a1=Q 11.Qh8+ skewers along the long diagonal and the queen on a1 falls.
ex.e17: Study by Khachaturov, 1947, on an idea by Grigoriev. Two pawns against two, and every move is the only one. Find the winning move.
ex.e17.hint: Make the black king spend moves. Where does the f-pawn queen, and what happens if the black king is on the eighth rank when the h-pawn arrives?
ex.e17.solution: 1.f5! (the f-pawn would queen with check), and after 1...Kc5, 2.h5! After 2...g3, 3.Ke1! (3.Ke2? allows d3 with check). The technique: every time the black king moves, a white pawn advances: 4.f6, 5.h6, 6.Kf2, 7.f7, 8.h7. After 8...g1=Q+ 9.Kxg1 d2, 10.f8=Q+! offers the queen: 10...Kxf8 and 11.h8=Q+ is born with check and arrives in time to stop the d-pawn.
ex.e18: Study by Moravec, 1950. Taking the d-pawn at once looks obvious. Is it? Find the draw.
ex.e18.hint: Count until Black queens on e1 and the white king goes to c8. Where does the deciding check come from, and who can block that line?
ex.e18.solution: 1.Kd5! After 1.Kxd6? e4 2.c4 e3 3.c5 e2 4.c6 e1=Q 5.Kd7 Qd1+ 6.Kc8 and 6...Qg4+ wins. 1.Kd5 threatens 2.Ke4 to stop the e-pawn, and the black king comes to f3: after 2.Kxd6 and the same race (6.Kd7 Qd1+ 7.Kc8), the black king on f3 blocks the d1–g4 diagonal and the c-pawn holds the draw.
key.race: Both pawns queen, but White gets there first, and the new queen in the corner already watches the square where the black pawn wants to queen. Counting is not enough: you must see what the queen does next.
key.check: The white pawn queens with check, because the black king stands on the same diagonal as the queening square. With that extra move, the queen is in time to stop the other pawn.
key.control: The white pawn queens in the corner, and the new queen controls the black pawn's queening square from afar. Promoting to anything but a queen would throw the win away.
key.skewer: Both sides queen and there are two queens on the board. A check along the line of Black's king and queen skewers the king, and the queen behind it falls.
key.catch: Running is not always best: here the white king first hunts down the black pawn, and the white edge pawn then queens on its own, because the black king is too far away.
key.diagonal: Black cannot simply run: if the pawn goes all the way, White queens with check. The black king must turn back and capture the white pawn first.
key.petrosianFischer: Petrosian against Fischer, 1958, in the position where they agreed a draw. The black rook, which is also on the board, can give itself up for one white pawn: the other one queens, but Black's bishop pawn reaches the last square but one with its king beside it, and the queen cannot win against that.
key.alatortsev: Alatortsev against Chekhover, 1937: Black's bishop pawn was still one square further back. That square gave the queen time to bring the white king closer, and White won.
history: In a pawn race each side has a free pawn and both run to queen. It seems to be just a matter of counting squares, and many players lose here by counting wrong or stopping too soon: whoever queens first may still not win, and whoever queens second sometimes loses the new queen to a check. The basic tool is the rule of the square, which every endgame book teaches. In 1958 Petrosian and Fischer, two future world champions, agreed a draw in an ending like this, because Fischer's pawn would get too close to queening for the queen to win. In 1937 Alatortsev beat Chekhover in a similar race, because there the pawn was one square further back. One square made all the difference.
practice: Now the practical challenge: an a-pawn against a g-pawn, with the black king on f3. Count, race with the double step and use the check when the queen is born. Pick your time control and go.
